messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: help on Wiener doc
parts:
There was a note to update the doc, but I don't understand what's
a comment about what's in Stan and what's a comment about what should
be in Stan.

When it says "prefer it in Stan" is that a suggestion to define a
different density than the one we have? Or is that what was implemented?

If someone can write up what should get dropped in as a paragraph in
the doc, drop it into this issue

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/issues/1617

and I'll get it into the doc. If that issue's closed, put it in the
next doc issue.

- Bob

P.S. Here's the note:

From Joachim Vandekerckhove on stan-users:

Sorry I'm a little late to this party, I had a long summer of travel. The reason we originally implemented the lower-bound hits as negative reaction times was to have a cheap way of encoding what is essentially a bivariate distribution (strictly positive RT and binary response). Because both the RT and the outcome are random variables, the current implementation (with only one bound) isn't entirely satisfactory if at any point we want to generate random numbers from the distribution.

I always liked the negative-RT solution even though it's a little counter-intuitive. I'd probably prefer it in Stan since it's how it works in JAGS... but the more conventional solution would be to make it actually bivariate, and let it operate on a [RT response] pair, where the first is a strictly positive real and the second is a boolean.

messages.author: 484c91357ac83f6b
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] help on Wiener doc
parts:
On 02/12/2015 00:04, Bob Carpenter wrote:
> There was a note to update the doc, but I don't understand what's
> a comment about what's in Stan and what's a comment about what should
> be in Stan.

I don't think there is anything in his comments meant to be added to the
manual.

> When it says "prefer it in Stan" is that a suggestion to define a
> different density than the one we have? Or is that what was implemented?

It refers to the author's original version, which is not exactly what is
implemented right now. His original code allowed random variables to be
negative or positive, while the current implementation only allows
positive random variables.

The wiener distribution we have models the amount of time it takes for a
Wiener process to reach an upper bound.

But there's also the possibility of modeling the amount of time it takes
to reach a lower bound. The author's original code modeled this
possibility (of lower bound) using negative random variables.

In the author's R package we do this using a variable resp:

#what you get in Stan
RWiener::dwiener(1.1, 2.1, .3, .55, .4, resp = "upper")

#this would be using -1.1 instead of 1.1 in his original implementation
for Stan
RWiener::dwiener(1.1, 2.1, .3, .55, .4, resp = "lower")

#sum of both densities, only this one integrates to one, wiener is
actually bivariate as he says
RWiener::dwiener(1.1, 2.1, .3, .55, .4, resp = "both")

> Because both the RT and the outcome are random variables, the current implementation (with only one bound) isn't entirely satisfactory if at any point we want to generate random numbers from the distribution.
>

This is interesting, but I'm not sure how well it would behave since
there is discontinuity in the derivatives when we change from lower to
upper (negative random variables to positive random variables).
